The third option describes `std::quick_exit` or `std::abort`.

questions.prompt: Which of these definitions of `main` is well-formed in C++23?
questions.explanation: `main` must have a declared return type of `int`, and a trailing return type counts as declaring it, so `auto main() -> int` is fine. Falling off the end of `main` is equivalent to `return 0;`, so the empty body is fine too. A deduced return type is not a declared `int`, and `main` may not be `static`, `inline`, `constexpr` or `consteval`; GCC rejects all three of the others.

questions.explanation: [stmt.dcl] says that if the initialization of a block-scope static exits by an exception, the variable is not initialized, and initialization is attempted again the next time control enters the declaration. The first two calls throw, the third succeeds and sets `v` to 30, and the last two calls skip the initializer. `1` would be right only if a failed initialization were never retried.

options: The relative order of `handler` and the destructors is unspecified
questions.explanation: The three dynamic initializations are ordered by definition in one file: `a` completes, then `handler` is registered, then `b` completes. [basic.start.term] runs destructors and `atexit` functions as one sequence in reverse: what completed after a registration is destroyed before that handler runs, and what completed before it is destroyed after. So `~b`, `handler`, `~a`. Treating `atexit` handlers as a separate stack gives either of the first two answers.

questions.prompt: When this program calls `std::quick_exit(0)`, which of the following run?
questions.explanation: `std::quick_exit` calls the functions registered with `at_quick_exit` in reverse order of registration and then calls `std::_Exit`. It destroys no objects and calls no `atexit` handlers, and whether `_Exit` flushes streams is implementation-defined, which is why the handler flushes `stdout` itself. The second and third options mix in parts of `std::exit`.

questions.prompt: Two files, `a.cpp` and `b.cpp`, are linked into one program. When `main` starts, what is the value of `x`?
options: Unspecified: 0 or 5, depending on which file is initialized first
Undefined behavior: `y` is read before its initialization
questions.explanation: `y` is constant-initialized, and [basic.start.static] says all static initialization strongly happens before any dynamic initialization. So `y` already holds 5 when the dynamic initializer of `x` calls `f`, whichever file's dynamic initialization runs first. The unspecified answer would be right if `y` had a dynamic initializer, such as `int y = compute();`.

questions.prompt: These are the only definitions in one file. What does the C++23 standard say about the value of `d2` once initialization is complete?
options: It is 0.0, because `d2` is initialized before `d1` in the same file
It is unspecified whether it is 0.0 or 1.0
It is 1.0, because `fd()` can be evaluated at compile time
Undefined behavior: `d1` is read before its lifetime begins
questions.explanation: Both variables have dynamic initializers, since `fd` is not `constexpr`. But [basic.start.static] lets an implementation perform a dynamic initialization statically when the result is the same, and doing that for `d1` is allowed. If it does, `d2` sees 1.0; if not, `d2` is initialized first and sees the zero-initialized 0.0. This is the standard's own example; GCC and Clang give 0.0, which is why the first option is tempting. There is no undefined behavior, because a zero-initialized `double` may be read.

questions.prompt: The exception escapes `main` and no handler exists. Is the destructor of `local` guaranteed to run?
options: Yes: the stack is always unwound before `std::terminate` is called
No: it is guaranteed not to run, because `std::terminate` is called at the throw
Undefined behavior: throwing out of `main` is not allowed
It is implementation-defined whether the stack is unwound before `std::terminate` is called
questions.explanation: When no matching handler is found, [except.handle] says `std::terminate` is called and whether the stack is unwound first is implementation-defined. GCC does not unwind, so `~T` is not printed there, but another implementation may unwind. This is why long-running programs catch everything in `main` when they need destructors to run.
